abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The incorporation of the current immunotherapy, GD2-targeting monoclonal antibodies, into the standard of care has moderately improved clinical outcomes in children with high-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NB); however, overall survival remains low. More than 50% of patients with HR-NB are refractory to or eventually develop resistance to anti-GD2 treatment. HR-NBs are generally known to have a low tumor mutational burden, are immunologically cold and possess an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Understanding the mechanisms of immune evasion may provide novel targets for improving the efficacy of immunotherapies for these immunologically cold HR-NBs. Here, utilizing immunocompetent mouse models of immunologically cold HR-NB, we revealed a novel function of IGF2BP1 in promoting the immune escape of neuroblastoma tumors. We demonstrate that neuroblastoma cell-specific knockdown of IGF2BP1 favorably alters the tumor microenvironment of HR-NBs, turning these “immunologically cold” tumors into an immunogenic type, thereby priming them for anti-GD2 therapy-induced immune responses. Downregulation of IGF2BP1 in NB cells decreased the number of immunosuppressive T-regulatory and dysfunctional/exhausted CD8+ T cells and promoted the accumulation of effector MHCII + macrophages at the tumor site. Importantly, knockdown of IGF2BP1 along with anti-GD2 immunotherapy induced a synergistic immunogenic effect and achieved a potent antitumor response in an HR-NB mouse model, with increased accumulation of effector CD8+ T cells and CD86+ macrophages but decreased MDSC numbers in the tumor microenvironment. Thus, disrupting NB cancer cell IGF2BP1-mediated immunosuppression is a potential approach for improving the efficacy of anti-GD2 immunotherapy towards HR-NBs.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, which originates from the progenitor cells of the sympathetic nervous system.1 NBs present a wide range of clinical variability, with low-to-intermediate risk groups exhibiting spontaneous regression and favorable prognosis, while increased therapeutic resistance and relapse observed in the high risk (HR) group.2-4 Current treatment for patients with high-risk neuroblastomas (HR-NBs) include intensive multimodal chemotherapy, radiation, myeloablative chemo with stem cell transplant and anti-GD2 (Dinutuximab) immunotherapy.2,3 However, the overall survival for this HR group remains low, thus accounting for 15% of cancer-related mortalities in children.5 Although the current anti-GD2 immunotherapy by itself or in combination with immunostimulatory agents has moderately improved the outcomes for patients with HR-NBs,6 more than 50% of these patients eventually develop resistance towards anti-GD2 treatment.7-9 Loss of GD2 expression and antibody internalization by target NB cells have been reported as some of the major mechanisms of GD2-immunotherapy escape in NB.10 Moreover, HR-NBs in general are characterized as immunologically cold tumors due to limited T-cell infiltration, downregulation of MHC I molecules, and a low mutational burden,5,11 rendering them insensitive to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Recent progress has been made in the areas of using haploidentical stem-cell transplants with anti-GD2 agents or in designing anti-GD2 CAR-T cells and anti-GD2/anti-CD3 bispecific armed T cells,12-14 but currently, no widely accepted, effective treatment options exist for patients with therapy-resistant NBs.15 Thus, identifying novel therapeutic targets or designing new combination strategies is essential for effectively treating refractory and clinically resistant HR-NBs. A few well-known oncogenic drivers of NB include MYCN amplification,3 chromosomal aberrations such as 1p loss,16 11q loss17,18 and 17q gain,19,20 which have been individually linked with poor outcomes. Among these, 17q gain is found in more than 50% of all NB cases and is associated with poor survival.16,19,20 IGF2BP1 is a putative oncogene at this frequently amplified 17q21 locus and was found to be highly expressed specifically in patients with advanced-stage NB.21 The oncogenic and prometastatic roles of IGF2BP1 in NB progression have been recently established.22,23 IGF2BP1 is a posttranscriptional regulator that binds and stabilizes several oncogenic transcripts,24,25 including MYCN,21,23 SEMA3A and SHMT2 in NB.22 Importantly, SEMA3A, which is known to regulate the immune microenvironment in multiple cancer types,26,27 was found to mediate the prometastatic function of IGF2BP1 in NB.22 Thus, we hypothesized the importance of IGF2BP1 in regulating the primary tumor microenvironment in NB.

Here, we identified the role of IGF2BP1 in mediating the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in HR-NBs, utilizing immunocompetent mice bearing “cold” GD2-expressing M1 and 9464D-NB tumors that simulate clinically high-risk disease. We show that depletion of IGF2BP1 in NB cells favorably alters the immune microenvironment of NB tumors, thereby turning these immunologically cold and immunosuppressive tumors into a more immunogenic type. Mechanistically, knocking down IGF2BP1 in NB cells reduced the accumulation of immunosuppressive regulatory CD4+ T cells (Tregs) and exhausted dysfunctional CD8+ T lymphocytes but increased the infiltration of MHCII-expressing effector macrophages at the tumor site. Furthermore, knocking down IGF2BP1 in combination with anti-GD2 (dinutuximab) antibody treatment synergistically improved the immune microenvironment by promoting the accumulation of activated effector (CD8+ ) and memory (CD4+ ) T lymphocytes and effector (CD86+ ) macrophages at the primary tumor site. Moreover, the combination of IGF2BP1 depletion with anti-GD2 treatment significantly decreased the tumor burden in mice and prolonged their survival. Our findings reveal the immunoregulatory role of IGF2BP1 in NB and demonstrate the dependency of these cold HR-NB tumors on IGF2BP1 for immune evasion. Importantly, in addition to the well-known NK cell-driven action of anti-GD2, we reveal a novel macrophage- and CD8+ T-cell-mediated mechanism of anti-GD2 immunotherapy that relies on IGF2BP1 depletion.

Overall, our study demonstrates the therapeutic benefit of targeting IGF2BP1 in combination with the current anti-GD2 immunotherapy in immunologically cold HR-NB murine models and proposes this novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of refractory/resistant NBs.

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: Mouse NB cell line – 9464D was a gift from Dr. Paul Sondel’s laboratory (University of Wisconsin), and the M1-NB cell line was generated in our laboratory from a liver-derived tumor of 9464D-IV-injected mouse.22,28 Both cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; VWR International) supplemented with 10% v/v FBS (Gibco by Life Technologies) and 100 units/ml penicillin and streptomycin (Corning). 9464D-GD2 and M1-GD2 expressing cells were generated by transducing 9464D and M1 cells with lentiviral particles harboring GD2/GD3 synthase (pCDH1-CMV-St8sia1-2A-B4galnt1-SV40-Hygro29), followed by hygromycin selection (500 µg/ml). The surface expression of GD2 was validated by flow cytometry staining, as previously described28 (Supplementary Figure 1, 2A). Briefly, 1 × 106 cells were washed sequentially with PBS and FACS buffer, followed by antibody staining with FITC anti-human ganglioside GD2 (BioLegend Cat# 357314, RRID:AB_2800977) for 30 min on ice in the dark. The cells were then washed (1500 rpm, 5 min) twice with 150 µl of FACS buffer, fixed with 200 µl of 2% paraformaldehyde for 20 min on ice, and resuspended in 300 µl of FACS buffer. Human NB cells – SK-N-AS were used as a positive control for GD2 expression. Data were acquired on a BD LSRFortessa (BD Biosciences, San Jose, Calif.) flow cytometer, and analyzed using FlowJo v.10.8.1 software.

IGF2BP1-KD and OE lines: shIGF2BP1 and shNT – M1 (GD2-expressing) cells were generated using doxycycline inducible SMARTvector Inducible TurboGFP shRNA lentiviral constructs (GE Dharmacon Cat# V3SM11256–03EG140486) and shRNA SMARTvector-inducible nontargeting control construct (GE Dharmacon Cat# VSC11654), respectively, as previously described.22 4−6 µg/ml doxycycline (6 days of treatment) was used for shRNA induction (supplementary Figure 2B). 9464D-GD2-transduced cells were used for ectopic expression of IGF2BP1. Stable clones of 9464D(GD2)-IGF2BP1 OE or 9464D(GD2)-EGFP-control were generated using LV-GFP-hIMP1 (pLKO. hIMP1_3G from Dr. Joel Yisraeli’s Lab) and EGFP-pReceiver LV105 (Genecopoeia Cat# EX-GFP-Lv105-B) constructs, respectively, via lentiviral transduction as previously described.22 Positive cells with GFP-tagged IGF2BP1 expression were obtained by flow cytometry sorting on a FACSAria SORP (BD Biosciences, San Jose, Calif.), and IGF2BP1 overexpression was verified by western blotting (Supplementary Figure 2B).

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Western blotting was performed as previously described.22,30 Briefly, 60 µg of total protein was separated on a 10% polyacrylamide/SDS gel, transferred to PVDF membranes, and the membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin (BSA) in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) (+ 0.1% Tween−20). The primary antibodies used were as follows: IGF2BP1 (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 8482, RRID:AB_11179079), CD68 (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 97778, RRID:AB_2928056), IL-6Rα (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 39837), PLCγ2 (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 3872, RRID:AB_2299586) and β-Actin (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 4970, RRID:AB_2223172). The horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody used was anti-rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling Technology Cat# 7074, RRID:AB_2099233).

sec.title: In vivo experiments
sec.p: All the animal procedures were performed in accordance with the conditions approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Pennsylvania State University College of Medicine. Six- to eight-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (RRID:IMSR _JAX:000664) were subcutaneously injected with either GD2-expressing shNT/shIGF2BP1- M1 (GD2) or EGFP/IGF2BP1-OE—9464D (GD2) cells (1 × 106 cells/mouse). The mice to be implanted with shNT/shIGF2BP1-M1 cells were switched to 200 mg/kg doxycycline feed (Bio-Serv # S3888) two days prior to cell injection. Upon the appearance of palpable tumors (15−20 mm3 in volume), the mice from each cell-injected group were equally randomized into either treatment group – anti-GD2 or isotype IgG control. Treatment consisted of 3 times a week IV-administration (via tail-vein) of anti-GD2 (Clone: 14G2a, BioXCell Cat# BE0318, RRID: AB_2819045)/IgG2a isotype control (Clone: C1.18.4, BioXCell Cat# BE0085, RRID: AB_1107771) (50 µg/mouse/dose in 100 µl of PBS) until the control group reached the experimental endpoint of tumor sizes ≥30 mm in diameter (either length or width), after which the treatments were discontinued, and the remaining mice were monitored for tumor growth and survival. Survival was determined by the humane experimental endpoint of a tumor size ≥30 mm in diameter. Mice were euthanized by the gradual introduction of CO2 in a closed chamber, with the flow rate adjusted to displace 30%−70% of the chamber volume per minute, as per the AVMA guidelines. Following the cessation of respiration, cervical dislocation was performed as a secondary method of euthanasia to ensure death. For CD8 depletion, an αCD8 antibody (Clone: 2.43, BioXCell Cat# BE0061, RRID: AB_1125541)/isotype-Rat IgG2b, k (Clone: LTF-2, BioXCell Cat# BE0090, RRID: AB_1107780) was administered intraperitoneally, with a first dose of 400 µg/mouse 2 days prior to starting the anti-GD2 treatment, followed by subsequent doses of 200 µg/mouse once a week for 3−4 weeks. The mice were monitored for tumor growth via caliper measurements every other day (tumor volume (mm3) calculated by formula = 0.5 × length × width2), followed by survival analysis (Kaplan‒Meier curve). n = 7−8 animals per group, with equal numbers of males and females used for tumor growth and survival studies. Mouse experimental design briefing cell-implantation and treatments is indicated in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Immune profiling of tumors by flow cytometry
sec.p: For immune profiling of tumors, a separate cohort of mice was subcutaneously injected with GD2-expressing shNT control or shIGF2BP1-M1 (GD2) cells, and tumors were harvested 4 weeks after cell injection. To study the effect of the IGF2BP1 depletion + anti-GD2 combination on the NB TME, mice bearing shNT/shIGF2BP1 tumors were treated with either IgG or anti-GD2 for 3 weeks (3 times a week, 25 µg/mouse/dose), followed by tumor harvesting for flow cytometry analysis. Harvested tumors were minced and digested using a collagenase‒DNAse mixture (1 mg/ml collagenase + 50 U/ml DNAse I in RPMI supplemented with 2% FBS) by incubation at 370 on a rocker for 30 min. The digested tissues were passed through 70 µm mesh screens using a 5 ml syringe plunger to prepare single-cell suspensions. The cell suspensions were centrifuged (500xg, 5 minutes), and the cell pellets were then resuspended in 1X RBC lysis buffer (eBioscience, Cat. no. 00-4300-54) (room temperature, 5 min) for red blood cell lysis. After the RBC lysis buffer was neutralized and the cells were washed with RPMI medium supplemented with 2% FBS, 2−2.5 × 106 cells were stained for lymphoid and myeloid cell markers, using a standard flow-staining protocol. Briefly, the cells were washed twice with PBS, blocked for nonspecific binding using anti-mouse CD16/CD32 Fc block (BD Biosciences, AB_394656) and stained with the live/dead fixable viability dye Alexa Fluor 780 (15 mins, RT in the dark). Following Fc block and live/dead staining, the cells were washed once with FACS buffer (PBS with 2% FBS + 0.1% sodium azide) and stained with the indicated antibody panels below at room temperature for 15 min in the dark (at a 1:100 dilution).

Lymphoid panel: CD45.2, CD3e, CD4, CD8a, NK1.1, CD62L, CD44 and Nrp1. Myeloid panel: CD45.2, lineage neg (CD3, CD19, NK1.1), CD11b, CD11c, F4/80, Ly6C, Ly6G, MHCII and CD86. Following antibody staining, the cells were washed three times with FACS buffer and fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde (20 min at 40 in the dark). An additional panel for regulatory T cells included surface staining for CD45.2, CD3e, CD4, CD25, and Nrp1 and intracellular staining for FoxP3, which was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Invitrogen, FoxP3/Transcription factor staining buffer kit, cat. no. 00-5523). Detailed antibody information is listed in Supplementary Table 2. Data were acquired on a 23 Color BD FACSymphony A3 (BD Biosciences, San Jose, Calif.) instrument at Penn State College of Medicine’s Flow Cytometry Core and analyzed using FlowJo v.10.8.1 software. The gating strategies are shown in Supplementary Figures 4 and 5A.

sec.title: Library preparation and sequencing of mRNA
sec.p: Three biological replicates of shIGF2BP1 and shNT – M1 cells were collected on day 6 after shRNA induction, and total RNA was extracted using Direct-zol™ RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research). The optical density values of the extracted RNA were measured using NanoDrop (Thermo Scientific) to confirm that the A260:A280 ratio was greater than 1.9. The RNA integration number (RIN) was measured using BioAnalyzer RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent Technologies). RNA-seq was conducted at the Penn State College of Medicine Genome Sciences core (RRID:SCR_021123). cDNA libraries were prepared using the Illumina® Stranded mRNA Prep Ligation Kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, polyA RNA was purified from 600 ng of total RNA using oligo (dT) beads. The extracted mRNA fraction was subjected to fragmentation, reverse transcription, end repair, 3’-end adenylation, and adaptor ligation, followed by PCR amplification and magnetic bead purification (Omega Bio-Tek). The unique dual index sequences (IDT® for Illumina® RNA UD Indexes Set A, Ligation, Illumina) were incorporated into the adaptors for multiplexed high-throughput sequencing. The final product was assessed for its size distribution and concentration using BioAnalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Kit (Agilent Technologies). The libraries were pooled and diluted to 3 nM with 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5, and then denatured using the Illumina protocol. The denatured libraries were loaded onto an S1 flow cell on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) and run for 2X53 cycles according to the manufacturer's instructions.

sec.title: Differential gene expression and pathway analysis
sec.p: De-multiplexed and adapter-trimmed sequencing reads were generated using Illumina bcl2fastq (released version 2.20.0.422), allowing no mismatches in the index read. BBDuk (sourceforge.net/projects/bbmap/) was used to trim/filter low-quality sequences using “qtrim = lr trimq = 10 maq = 10” option. Next, alignment of the filtered reads to the mouse reference genome (GRCm38) was done using HISAT2 (version 2.1.0)31, with --no-mixed and --no-discordant options. Read counts were calculated using HTSeq32 by supplementing Ensembl gene annotation (GRCm38.78). EdgeR33 was used to fit the read counts to the negative binomial model along with a generalized linear model (GLM), and differentially expressed genes were determined via the likelihood ratio test method implemented in the edgeR package. Significance was defined as a q-value <0.05 was calculated via the Benjamini‒Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate (FDR). The ggplot2 R package34 was used to generate a heatmap. These significantly differentially expressed genes (p-adjusted values <0.05) were further analyzed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, QIAGEN Inc., https://digitalinsights.qiagen.com/IPA) to identify associated cellular processes and canonical pathways, and construct gene interaction networks.35

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: GraphPad Prism 10.4 was used for statistical analysis. Unpaired two-tailed t-tests were used for two group comparisons, and one-way ANOVA was used for comparing multiple groups. Two-way ANOVA or a mixed model was used to compare the tumor growth rates. The data are presented as the means ± SEMs. Survival curves were generated using the Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Statistical significance is indicated in the graphs as well as in the figure legends (significance level: α = 0.05).

sec.title: Depletion of IGF2BP1 sensitizes NB tumors to anti-GD2 immunotherapy in mouse HR-NB models
sec.p: Although the most recent anti-GD2 immunotherapy has improved patient outcomes, the survival benefit in the HR group is still modest due to increased immunotherapeutic resistance.7,8 Moreover, owing to intense treatment, most surviving patients suffer from adverse effects such as neuropathy, fever, and myelosuppression.15,36 Thus, to identify strategies that can enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy, we first examined the potential of targeting IGF2BP1 (the newly identified driver of NB progression) in combination with anti-GD2 immunotherapy against NB tumors. GD2-expressing M1 cells (GD2 surface expression validated in Supplementary Figure 1) transduced with IGF2BP1-specific shRNA (shIGF2BP1) or nontargeting shRNA control (shNT) were subcutaneously injected into syngeneic C57BL/6 mice. The animals were subsequently randomized into either the anti-GD2 immunotherapy group or the IgG control treatment group, after which they were subjected to tumor growth and survival analyses (Figure 1A). As expected, and consistent with our previous data, depletion of IGF2BP1 alone (without anti-GD2 treatment) had no significant effect on primary tumor growth22 compared to the shNT + IgG control group (Figure 1B). Similarly, individual anti-GD2 treatment also failed to reduce the growth of these aggressive HR-NB, M1 tumors (Figure 1B). However, NB cell-specific knockdown of IGF2BP1, along with anti-GD2 antibody treatment, significantly delayed tumor growth in mice relative to the other individual determinant groups (Figure 1B). Moreover, survival analysis, specifically comparing the two groups subjected to anti-GD2 treatment with or without IGF2BP1 knockdown, revealed significantly prolonged survival in the IGF2BP1-KD + anti-GD2 mice compared to the shNT control cell-injected mice treated with the anti-GD2 antibody (Figure 1C), thus suggesting the potential of targeting IGF2BP1 to increase the antitumor efficacy of anti-GD2 immunotherapy. We further validated these findings and the observed dependency of the therapeutic efficacy of anti-GD2 agents on IGF2BP1 expression, utilizing relatively less aggressive 9464D cells (GD2/GD3 synthase-transduced, Supplementary Figure 2A) than M1 cells, by overexpressing (OE) IGF2BP1 in these cells. Consistently, anti-GD2 treatment delayed tumor growth in 9464D-EGFP control cell-injected mice but failed to do so in 9464D-IGF2BP1 OE cell-injected mice (Figure 1D). Taken together, these results indicate the dependency of NB tumors on IGF2BP1 expression and that depleting IGF2BP1 in NB sensitizes these NB tumors to anti-GD2 therapy, thereby increasing the efficacy of the current anti-GD2 immunotherapy. This finding suggests potential targeting of IGF2BP1 along with anti-GD2 therapy as a novel treatment approach for NBs with primary or acquired resistance to GD2 immunotherapy.

sec.title: IGF2BP1 mediates an immunosuppressive microenvironment in NB tumors
sec.p: With its ability to affect the efficacy of anti-GD2 therapy and its previously identified function in regulating the microenvironment of metastatic sites,22 we hypothesized that IGF2BP1 contributes to the regulation of the primary tumor microenvironment (TME) in NB. Moreover, using the TIDE (tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion) algorithm,37 we found that increased IGF2BP1 expression was associated with increased death risk due to its correlation with immune cell dysfunction (survival risk score, Supplementary Figure 3A) and reduced cytotoxic T-cell infiltration (cytotoxic T-lymphocyte levels, Supplementary Figure 3B) in (treatment naive) neuroblastoma patient datasets. TIDE is a transcriptome biomarker database that models tumor immune evasion and predicts immunotherapy response by analyzing gene expression profiles to assess T-cell dysfunction and exclusion.37 To examine the effect of IGF2BP1 on tumor immune cell infiltration, primary tumors from shNT-M1- or shIGF2BP1-M1 cell injected mice were isolated and processed for flow cytometry analysis (Figure 2A). We found that the shIGF2BP1-M1 tumors had significantly lower numbers of Nrp1-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells than the shNT-M1 tumors did (Figure 2B−D), with no significant differences observed in the total number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Supplementary Figure 5B). As previously reported, Nrp1 is expressed specifically on T-regs and exhausted, dysfunctional effector lymphocytes38-40 and thus is used here as a marker for identifying nonfunctional/terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells and suppressive regulatory T cells. Similarly, knockdown of IGF2BP1 resulted in substantially decreased numbers of FoxP3+ , CD25+ and FoxP3+ , CD25- regulatory T cells (T-regs) relative to those in shNT control tumors (Figure 2E, F), and showed significantly increased effector T-cell (CD4+ or CD8+ ) to T-reg (FoxP3+ CD25+ ) cell ratios (Supplementary Figure 5C). Both subsets of T-regs, FoxP3+ CD25+ and FoxP3+ CD25-, additionally expressed Nrp1 on a subset of cells in the shNT-M1 tumors (Figure 2E). The higher number of Nrp1+ CD4 and CD8 cells, and T-regs in shNT tumors thus indicate the immunosuppressive characteristic of NB tumors, which is altered and relieved upon IGF2BP1 depletion. Moreover, IGF2BP1-KD also increased the infiltration of CD11b+, Ly6C+, MHCII hi, F4/80+ cells, which are identified as effectors and potentially antigen-presenting macrophages (Figure 2G, H) and (Supplementary Figure 5D). Overall, these results indicate the role of IGF2BP1 in promoting an immunosuppressive microenvironment in NB tumors.

sec.title: IGF2BP1 knockdown along with anti-GD2 immunotherapy has a synergistic immunogenic effect on NB TME
sec.p: Anti-GD2 antibody (dinutuximab) is known to mediate antitumor effects by triggering complement-dependent cytotoxicity, recruiting NK cells that induce antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, activating phagocytic macrophages, and stimulating macrophage-mediated phagocytosis.15 Our above data indicate increased infiltration of MHCII+ macrophages and decreased accumulation of immunosuppressive/dysfunctional lymphocytes in NB tumors in response to IGF2BP1 knockdown (Figure 2). Moreover, the combination of IGF2BP1 inhibition with anti-GD2 treatment had a synergistic antitumor effect in mice (Figure 1B, C). These findings prompted us to examine whether NB cell-specific depletion of IGF2BP1 enhances the ability of anti-GD2 antibodies to regulate the NB immune microenvironment. Mice bearing shNT control/shIGF2BP1-M1 tumors were treated with either anti-GD2 or isotype IgG antibodies, followed by flow cytometry analysis of the tumor suspensions (Figure 3A). shIGF2BP1 tumors treated with anti-GD2 antibody showed increased levels of CD4 and CD8 T cells that were negative for the CD62L marker and expressed the activation marker CD44. CD62L is a well-known naïve and central memory T cell marker that is shed from the cell membrane upon activation, while CD44 is a classic marker of T cell activation and has been used to distinguish memory and effector T cells from their naïve counterparts. We detected significantly higher infiltration of activated, effector CD8+ T cells in response to IGF2BP1 KD combined with anti-GD2 treatment than in the individual IGF2BP1 KD or anti-GD2 treatment groups (Figure 3B, C). Similarly, increased numbers of CD44+ , and CD62L- CD4 cells were found in the combination group with IGF2BP1 KD and anti-GD2 treatment (Figure 3D, E), suggesting the accumulation of effector and effector memory T cells in these tumors. The other major population of CD4 cells found was CD44low, CD62L- (Quadrant 4, Figure 3E), which might be a subset of effector memory T-cells that play a role in tissue-resident memory.41,42 Moreover, we observed an increased population of effector, CD86-expressing macrophages in the tumors of the combination (IGF2BP1 KD + anti-GD2) group of mice (Figure 3F, Supplementary Figure 5E). CD86 is expressed on antigen-presenting cells, including effector macrophages, which provide costimulatory signals for cytotoxic T-cell activation and survival. Importantly, antitumor M1-like macrophages are known to express high levels of CD86 and MHCII molecules. In contrast, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which are negative for MHCII and CD86 expression, were found at reduced levels in response to IGF2BP1 KD alone than in shNT-M1 tumors with or without anti-GD2 treatment (Figure 3G, Supplementary Figure 5F), indicating that inhibition of IGF2BP1 promotes the activation of MDSCs to effector macrophages in NB tumors. Anti-GD2 treatment along with IGF2BP1 depletion further reduced the accumulation of (CD11b+ , Ly6C+ ) F4/80-, MHCII- cells (MDSCs) (although not significantly lower than shIGF2BP1 alone) (Figure 3G).

sec.title: IGF2BP1 depletion increases the anti-tumor activity of GD2 immunotherapy via CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes
sec.p: To validate the above-identified IGF2BP1-associated immune mechanism in the NB TME, we examined whether CD8+ cells are required for improved antitumor immunity following the knockdown of IGF2BP1. We thus specifically depleted CD8+ cells (using an anti-CD8a neutralizing antibody) to examine whether this depletion could rescue the ability of IGF2BP1 to sustain tumor growth. Mice subcutaneously injected with either shNT/shIGF2BP1 – M1 cells were randomized into different treatment groups: IgG (isotype control for anti-GD2), anti-GD2, anti-GD2+ IgG2b (isotype control for anti-CD8), or anti-GD2+ anti-CD8, followed by tumor growth monitoring and survival analysis. Consistent with our previous results, shIGF2BP1 – M1 tumor-bearing mice treated with the anti-GD2 antibody presented a significant delay in tumor growth (Figure 4A) and thus survived longer (Figure 4B) than did mice bearing shNT—M1 tumors with or without anti-GD2 antibody treatment or shIGF2BP1 cell-injected mice in the IgG-control group. Importantly, anti-CD8 Abs abolished the tumoricidal effect of this combination (IGF2BP1 KD + anti-GD2) (Figure 4A, B), indicating the requirement for CD8+ T cells in antitumor immunity induced by the combination of IGF2BP1 inhibition and anti-GD2 treatment. Treatment with anti-CD8 (αCD8) restored tumor growth in mice bearing shIGF2BP1 tumors treated with anti-GD2 (Figure 4A), consequently reducing the survival of these mice (Figure 4B), relative to the shIGF2BP1 group treated with anti-GD2 (+IgG2b control). Overall, these results validate our identified immunoregulatory mechanism of IGF2BP1 in NB tumors, which is favorably altered upon IGF2BP1 knockdown and anti-GD2 treatment.

sec.title: Differential expression of immune-related genes in response to IGF2BP1 knockdown
sec.p: To determine whether additional signaling pathways are involved in regulating the tumor microenvironment via cancer-immune/stromal cell interactions that are regulated by IGF2BP1 in NB, we performed RNA sequencing on our shNT and shIGF2BP1 – M1(NB) cells. RNA-seq analysis revealed a substantial cluster of genes that were differentially regulated in response to IGF2BP1 knockdown (Supplementary Figure 6A, FDR < 0.05). These significantly differentially expressed genes were further analyzed using IPA (Ingenuity Pathway Analysis). Among the overrepresented cellular functions associated with the differentially regulated genes were cell-to-cell signaling & interaction, immune cell trafficking, and inflammatory responses (Supplementary Figure 6B). Moreover, several of the top affected canonical pathways consisted of immune regulation and cancer-stromal cell-to-cell interactions in the TME (Supplementary Figure 6C). Prominent negatively regulated pathways include macrophage alternative activation signaling, which induces M1 to M2 (anti-inflammatory type) polarization of macrophages; the STAT3 signaling pathway, which is known to inhibit the expression of proinflammatory cytokines and promote the production of immunosuppressive factors; the tumor microenvironment pathway, which consists of immunosuppressive cell-to-cell signaling between components of the TME; extracellular matrix organization; PDGF signaling, which is known to modulate fibroblasts; and the IL-6 signaling pathway, which is known to support tumor growth by evading immune surveillance. The upregulated pathways included TREM1 signaling, which is known to regulate diverse aspects of innate and adaptive immune responses by increasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines (such as TNF and GM-CSF). The regulatory network depicts the molecules and their predicted functions associated with immune cell regulation (Supplementary Figure 6D). Furthermore, of the top identified differentially regulated genes, we chose a few targets for protein validation, such as CD68, IL6ra (which were downregulated) and PLCg2 (upregulated) based on their functional relevance in immune-regulatory pathways. IL6ra (interleukin 6 receptor, alpha) is associated with the STAT3, IL-6, and tumor microenvironment pathways, and Plcg2 (phospholipase C, gamma 2) is associated with PDGF signaling and TREM1 signaling. CD68 is a tumor-associated macrophage (M2) antigen that imparts immunosuppressive ability to these tumor-supportive macrophages but is also known to be expressed by tumor cells to evade the antitumor effects of CTLs.43 Consistent with our RNA-Seq findings, CD68 and IL6ra protein levels were significantly lower in shIGF2BP1-M1 cells than in shNT-M1 cells, while Plcg2 protein levels were upregulated in response to IGF2BP1 KD (Supplementary Figure 7). Thus, the differential gene signature and associated pathways support our observed tumor immune profiles and suggest that depletion of IGF2BP1 in NB cells modulates TME-regulating pathways/factors, subsequently altering cancer-stromal cell interactions and signaling in the NB TME.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: An immunosuppressive TME plays a central role in imparting solid tumors with the ability to escape immune surveillance and develop resistance to immunotherapies via various mechanisms.44 In addition to physical barriers such as a dense extracellular matrix and aberrant vasculature that restrict effector T-cell infiltration, the immunosuppressive TME also presents a cytokine/chemokine milieu that preferentially recruits immunosuppressive cells, such as T regs, myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor-associated macrophages, which all inhibit cytotoxic T-cell function and activation.44-46 Most pediatric cancers, including NBs, are considered immunologically “cold” tumors due to their low mutation burden, resulting in low neoantigen expression and thus limited recognition by the adaptive immune system. HR-NBs evade antitumor immune responses through mechanisms including impaired cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, downregulation of MHCI expression, and accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells;5,15 however, the determinants regulating these processes have not yet been fully elucidated. Strategies for the selective immune recognition of tumor cells and the induction of antitumor immune responses, such as tumor-specific monoclonal antibodies against surface antigen-GD2, have been developed for NBs.15,36 Anti-GD2 immunotherapy has improved outcomes in HR-NB,6-9 resistance and adverse effects (e.g., neuropathy, immune-related toxicity) remain significant challenges.47 Therefore, enhancing its efficacy or designing novel combination therapies is crucial for improving clinical outcomes by enabling the selective targeting and maximization of the eradication of tumor cells and generating immune memory against minimal residual disease.

With the aim of developing an efficient therapeutic approach for treating patients with HR-NBs, we combined the anti-GD2-based approach (dinutuximab) with the selective targeting of tumor IGF2BP1, the newly identified oncogenic driver of NB progression,22,23 in immunocompetent mice bearing cold HR-NB tumors. We utilized M1-GD2 and 9464D-GD2 murine NB models, which simulate immunologically cold human HR-NBs and present a low tumor mutation burden and low MHCI expression.28

Collectively, our findings reveal the immunoregulatory role of IGF2BP1 in promoting an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in NBs and the dependence of these HR-NB tumors on IGF2BP1 for immune evasion. These findings are in line with our previous observations that IGF2BP1 plays an important role in regulating melanoma immunogenicity.48 We show that depletion of IGF2BP1 favorably alters the immune signature of NB tumors by reducing immunosuppressive lymphocyte infiltration and increasing the accumulation of effector macrophages at the tumor site, thereby alleviating the immunosuppressive microenvironment of NB tumors. The combination of NB cell-specific knockdown of IGF2BP1 with dinutuximab (anti-GD2) treatment synergistically induced an immunogenic effect by promoting the accumulation of activated CD8+ T-cells and antigen-presenting (CD86+ ) effector macrophages. Effector CD8+ T cells are the ultimate executors of antitumor immunity and are thus exploited for immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and adoptive T-cell-based therapies. These immunotherapies have shown considerable success in immunogenic cancer types;46 however, their efficacy is limited in “cold” tumors such as HR-NBs, which have fewer activated CD8+ T-cells and increased immunosuppressive cell infiltration.5,15 Current anti-GD2 immunotherapy primarily functions through CD8+ T cell-independent mechanisms, such as complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) via NK cell activation, and macrophage-mediated phagocytosis, increasing CD8+ T-cell infiltration and function, may further improve treatment efficacy for these cold tumors. Our results demonstrate that downregulation of IGF2BP1 results in these cold, immunosuppressive HR-NB tumors becoming more immunogenic by reducing the frequency of Tregs, thereby priming them for immunotherapy. Furthermore, knockdown of IGF2BP1 increased the abundance of effector CD8+ T lymphocytes. Importantly, and unusually for NB, CD8+ T lymphocytes mediate antitumor responses to anti-GD2 treatment in combination with IGF2BP1 inhibition, thus revealing the potential of utilizing this approach for native or adoptive T-cell-based treatments for HR-NBs. No significant differences in total, immature (CD27+ ) or effector (CD27-) NK cells were observed upon independently knocking down IGF2BP1 or in combination with anti-GD2 treatment (data not shown), indicating an NK cell-independent effect.

NB tumors are infiltrated with myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) that differentiate into protumor (M2-like) tumor-associated macrophages, which are known to suppress CD8+ T-cell responses and are associated with poor prognosis in patients with HR-NBs.49-51 Likewise, our HR-NB tumor-bearing mice showed increased accumulation of immature CD11b + , CD11c-/MHCII-/Ly6Chi myeloid cells at the tumor site, which were significantly reduced in IGF2BP1-KD tumors. Consistently, downregulation of IGF2BP1 independently or in combination with anti-GD2 treatment increased the infiltration of MHCII + and CD86+ effector macrophages within the tumor niche. Similar sizes of whole tumors (by volume) were utilized for flow analysis, and since these tumors from different experimental groups did not significantly vary in the proportion of CD45+ cells (Supplementary Figure 5G), the frequencies (percentages) of different immune cell subsets relative to either live CD45+ cells or their respective parent populations were used to determine the changes in the immune cell composition within the NB tumors in response to IGF2BP1 modulation or anti-GD2 treatment. A limitation of this approach is that it does not provide the absolute cell numbers in the sample; however, we do not expect to observe a different outcome with respect to absolute cell counts because of the similar proportions of CD45+ tumor immune cell infiltrates. Thus, the changing frequencies of different immune cell subsets indicate an altered TME in response to IGF2BP1 KD or anti-GD2 treatment.

IGF2BP1 knockdown in M1-NB cells revealed altered gene expression patterns, confirming our observed TME and immune profile changes. Specifically, downregulation of the macrophage alternative activation pathway, which is associated with M2 (anti-inflammatory, protumor) macrophage polarization, and activation of TREM1 signaling, which is linked to proinflammatory responses, indicated a shift toward the accumulation of effector macrophages (MHCII + , CD86+ ), supporting our observed myeloid cell phenotype in IGF2BP1-KD tumors. Concurrently, downregulation of IL-9, IL-15, and IL-27 signaling, all of which are implicated in inducing an immunosuppressive TME and immune evasion, was observed upon IGF2BP1 KD. IL-9, initially identified as a T and mast cell growth factor, was recently found to promote immune evasion in NSCLC via T-regs.52 Likewise, the proinflammatory cytokine IL-15 also promotes tumor progression; elevated intra-tumoral and circulating IL-15/IL-15Ra is associated with poor prognosis and immune evasion in multiple cancers, suggesting its pro-tumorigenic role by inducing an immunosuppressive TME.53,54 IL-27 similarly fosters tumor growth by inducing an immunosuppressive TME,55 and is associated with disease progression in various cancers.56,57 Mechanistically, IL-27 induces the expression of immune checkpoint molecules (Tim3, LAG3, PD-1, TIGIT) on CD8 T-cells, leading to their dysfunction.58 Disruption of IL-27R signaling rescued the cytotoxic anti-tumor activities of innate lymphocytes and alleviated TME immunosuppression in hepatic cancer.59 Furthermore, IL-27 signaling is crucial for the suppressive function of T-regs, contributing to the pro-tumorigenic activity of tumor-infiltrating T-regs.60 Additionally, upregulation of Angiopoietin 1 (ANG1), known for modulating endothelial and immune cells and promoting monocyte to M1-like pro-inflammatory macrophage differentiation,61 suggests IGF2BP1's role in stroma remodeling. TNFRSF9 (4-1BB), a key receptor involved in inflammation regulation and linked to T-cell exhaustion,62,63 was downregulated upon inhibition of IGF2BP1. Thus, alterations in these immunoregulatory genes and pathways in response to IGF2BP1 KD reflect the function of IGF2BP1 in cancer-stromal cell interactions within the NB TME. Another well-known mechanism of immune escape is the dysregulated expression of IFNγ receptor kinases, such as JAK1, JAK2 and STAT, in the TME. Importantly, STAT3 hyperactivation within tumor cells establishes an immunosuppressive microenvironment by downregulating immunostimulatory factors (e.g., IFNs and IL-12) and upregulating immunosuppressive cytokines/growth factors (e.g., IL-6, IL-1, TGFβ, and VEGF). These tumor-derived factors, such as IL-6, can also enhance STAT3 signaling in stromal and immune cells within the tumor niche, propagating immunosuppressive bidirectional crosstalk. Elevated STAT3 in the TME promotes the accumulation of immunosuppressive Tregs and M2 macrophage polarization, and inhibits CD8+ T cell cytolytic activity, thus facilitating immune evasion.64 Concordantly, our findings of downregulated IL-6, STAT3, and IL-1 pathways upon IGF2BP1 KD in NB cells further support the role of IGF2BP1 in fostering an immunosuppressive TME and promoting immune evasion in HR-NB. IGF2BP1 is an RNA-binding protein that binds and stabilizes its target mRNAs, including SEMA3A, SHMT222 and c-MYC, which have been shown to regulate immune responses,27,65,66 suggesting that IGF2BP1 functions in the TME by regulating the expression of immune-regulatory factors. Since IGF2BP1 plays a pleiotropic role by regulating the expression of multiple of its mRNA targets, the precise molecular mechanism underlying the observed TME phenotype is beyond the scope of this article and is currently underway.

Nonetheless, taken together, we establish the immunosuppressive role of IGF2BP1 in HR-NBs, demonstrate the dependency of NB tumors on IGF2BP1 for escape from GD2 immunotherapy, and identify the associated immune-cell regulatory mechanism. Overall, our preclinical findings demonstrate that targeting IGF2BP1 in combination with the current anti-GD2 treatment enhances the efficacy of this immunotherapy and thus provides a novel combination therapeutic approach for treating HR-NBs. Additionally, the altered immunoregulatory gene signature in M1-shIGF2BP1 NB cells further validated the IGF2BP1-mediated signaling between NB cells and stromal/noncancer cells in the NB tumor niche. Several specific experimental inhibitors of IGF2BP1 have recently been developed (reviewed in67, including our recently developed IGF2BP1 inhibitor, AVJ16,68), which holds promise for translating these findings into future treatments for resistant/relapsed HR-NBs. This represents a significant success in targeting RNA-binding proteins, and there is a concerted effort by our group and other groups to further optimize their delivery, bioavailability, and potency to be able to move them to clinical trials. Moreover, the observed novel - CD8+ T-cell-dependent mechanism of anti-GD2’s (dinutuximab’s) action, which relies on IGF2BP1 inhibition, could be imperative for future investigations to design adoptive/CAR T-cell therapies or additional combination immunotherapeutic strategies for NB treatment.
